text: As someone who works in security, I disagree! Security often comes at the cost of convenience, but it doesn't have to. My experience is mostly with IT security, but: * Passkeys are an example of technology that is both more convenient and more secure. In this case security comes at the price of (a bit of) privacy, though. * Memory-safe languages are much more convenient, and much more secure than unsafe ones. The price usually comes at a price of performance, but does not have to, and modern memory-safe languages are barely slower than C. * Prepared statements in databases are both more convenient and more secure than joining strings. The price is a bit more complexity. * OTP codes (google authenticator style) are at least as convenient as SMS codes, while being more secure. The price is... a bigger chance of locking yourself out, I guess. * Passphrases are easier to remember and more secure than passwords. And a password manager is even more secure. * Server-side HTML rendering with templates is much more secure and much more convenient than joining strings manually. * Using managed services (managed k8s, cloud storage, s3, hosted databases) is more convenient than self-hosting. Security depends on your threat model - but you need a proper infrastructure team to manage updates/hardening. For small companies it's not viable. * SSO with OIDC in corporate environment is more secure and more convenient for users and administrators than having a separate login everywhere. * Docker containers are more convenient (to work with) and more secure than running things on bare metal on physical servers. * Exceptions are easier to use and safer than signals, and as secure as return codes (different failure modes). * Automated updates are much more secure and much more convenient than having to manually trigger system update every time. * Building and deploying images with CI/CD is more convenient and much more secure than having developers deploy to production from a local machine. * Traditional banking is more secure and more convenient than cryptocurrencies (lol). I can go on. You may disagree with some of them, but surely you will agree that "more security = less convenience" is not an universal truth.

text: Bitcoin’s base layer is famous for its deliberate ossification, making protocol changes famously difficult to achieve. But what if developers could introduce powerful new capabilities—like covenants—without touching consensus rules? In Part 6 of Cointelegraph Research’s definitive series on Bitcoin Covenants, researchers examine a fascinating proposal: Functional Encryption (FE) Covenants. Traditionally, standard public-key cryptography allows a private key to sign any message. However, FE-based designs propose moving covenant behavior out of Bitcoin Script and directly into the signing key itself. By cryptographically restricting keys, only transactions that satisfy predefined spending conditions can ever be signed—allowing nodes to verify signatures using standard OP_CHECKSIG mechanisms without requiring a network-wide soft fork. While practical implementation hurdles remain, this approach opens up entirely new avenues for scaling and securing Bitcoin architecture. text: Institutions pile back into US Bitcoin ETFs in Q3 after selling streak. > Asset managers added the equivalent of 49,229 Bitcoin to their US Bitcoin ETF holdings in the third quarter, reversing three quarters of net selling. > > Institutional investment managers’ holdings of US Bitcoin exchange-traded funds climbed to a record high in the third quarter, as they reversed three straight quarters of net selling, according to regulatory filings. > > The 13F filings, analyzed by Galaxy Research, show that the reporting companies added an equivalent of 49,229 Bitcoin BTC > in the third quarter, outpacing the 47,054 Bitcoin they shed over the last three quarters combined. This lifted the reported total holdings to 356,491 BTC, the highest on record. > > “The quarter’s accumulation was the work of a few dozen large institutions,” wrote Galaxy’s head of firmwide research Alex Thorn. > > Quarterly 13F filings provide a point-in-time snapshot of US-listed securities held by reporting institutional investment managers. Thorn said half of the net addition of spot Bitcoin ETF shares came from advisors and wealth platforms. > > Wells Fargo posted the largest increase, adding the equivalent of 14,636 Bitcoin, making it the largest institutional holder of spot Bitcoin ETPs. Other strong gainers included Brevan Howard, Bank of America, Millennium Management and Jane Street. > > “Early readings suggest longer-term holders make up a growing share of the spot Bitcoin ETF investor base,” Bitwise analyst Camran Khosravi previously told Cointelegraph, when the first batch of 13F filings had begun to come in. > > The number of managers reporting a position in a spot Bitcoin ETF also rose for the first time in three quarters, increasing by 191 to 2,166. > > This all came as Bitcoin gained about 43% in the third quarter, ending September at $83,621. > > Meanwhile, Galaxy’s data shows BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust accounted for the largest share of holdings reported by 13F filers, with the equivalent of 232,453 BTC held by the filers. This was followed by the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund. > > Together, the two funds were responsible for 77% of all Bitcoin held by the reporting entities. > > US Bitcoin ETFs post two months of outflows > > The record institutional holdings in Q3 contrast with more recent weakness in US spot Bitcoin ETFs, with net monthly outflows reaching $515 million in October and $2.9 billion of outflows month to date, according to TFTC’s Bitcoin ETF tracker. > > Earlier in the month, Bitwise head of research André Dragosch told Cointelegraph he viewed the selling as “related to a short-term risk-off environment rather than a structural change in institutional sentiment.”
title: Institutions pile back into US Bitcoin ETFs in Q3 after selling streak

text: AllSwap Architecture: Solving Cross-Chain Liquidity Without Smart Contract Approvals or KYC. Cross-chain liquidity fragmentation remains one of the most stubborn bottlenecks in the decentralized ecosystem. Today, crypto users routinely navigate dozens of disparate Layer-1 and Layer-2 blockchains—such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, TRON, TON, Arbitrum, and Base. Yet, moving assets between these networks has historically exposed users to severe security vulnerabilities and systemic friction. Historically, users relied on two primary bridging rails: 1. **Centralized Exchanges (CEXs):** Require mandatory identity verification (KYC), custodial trust, withdrawal fees, and the constant threat of frozen accounts during market volatility. 2. **Standard Web3 Bridges:** Require users to connect browser extension wallets (MetaMask, Phantom) and sign token approval transactions (`approve()`), leaving wallets susceptible to malicious frontend injections, drainer scripts, and approval exploits. To eliminate both custodial exposure and wallet-connection attack vectors, **[AllSwap](https://allswap.io/)** (https://allswap.io/) introduces a streamlined, non-custodial cross-chain swap aggregator engineered around single-use deposit addresses. --- ### Key Innovations of AllSwap #### 1. Zero Wallet-Connection Risk Unlike conventional decentralized applications that prompt users to connect a browser wallet and grant smart contract approvals, AllSwap never connects to your wallet. Each order generated on https://allswap.io/ produces an ephemeral, single-use deposit address on the source network. Users transfer funds from any personal hardware wallet, mobile wallet, or exchange account. Once the deposit confirms on-chain, the swap engine routes the transaction and deposits native tokens directly into the receiving address. #### 2. Accountless and Privacy-Preserving Financial sovereignty requires privacy. AllSwap operates without sign-ups, passwords, or KYC document submissions. A cross-chain swap can be initiated and confirmed within minutes without establishing a centralized user profile. #### 3. Native Multi-Chain Coverage AllSwap aggregates liquidity across both EVM and non-EVM ecosystems, facilitating direct native swaps across: * **Bitcoin (BTC)** * **Ethereum (ETH & ERC-20 tokens)** * **Solana (SOL & SPL tokens)** * **TRON (TRX & TRC-20 USDT)** * **The Open Network (TON)** * **Layer-2 Networks:** Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, BNB Chain, and Polygon Whether converting TRC-20 USDT into native Solana or bridging Bitcoin directly into Base tokens, AllSwap handles the transaction in a single step without requiring users to acquire intermediate gas tokens. #### 4. Guaranteed Upfront Pricing Cross-chain transactions often suffer from opaque execution spreads and hidden slippage. AllSwap provides transparent quotes before any deposit is initiated. The guaranteed minimum output quote incorporates a flat **0.25% service fee** alongside actual on-chain gas costs. #### 5. Automatic Refund Protection To eliminate trapped liquidity during severe network congestion or sudden market price shifts, every swap requires a user-specified refund address on the origin network. If a transaction fails to complete, funds are automatically returned without requiring customer support tickets. --- ### How to Execute a Swap on AllSwap 1. **Select Pair & Network:** Visit [AllSwap.io](https://allswap.io/) and choose your source and destination cryptocurrencies. 2. **Provide Addresses:** Enter your destination receiving address and a source network fallback refund address. 3. **Send Deposit:** Transfer the specified amount to the generated one-time deposit address. Your swapped tokens will arrive directly in your receiving wallet. --- ### Quick Summary * **Official Website:** [https://allswap.io/](https://allswap.io/) * **Platform Type:** Non-Custodial Cross-Chain Swap & Bridge Aggregator * **Fee Structure:** Flat 0.25% service fee

text: Security in decentralized finance has always been a high-stakes balancing act. 🚨 A major new development on Ethereum is sparking intense industry debate. Phylax’s recently announced security system—integrated with top block builder Titan Builder—allows DeFi protocols to define rules that intercept and block potentially harmful transactions before they ever settle on the blockchain. The Case for Protection: By acting as an on-chain circuit breaker, the tool aims to stop multi-million-dollar exploits, hacks, and unauthorized vault drains dead in their tracks, offering a powerful defense against bad actors. The Censorship Concern: However, prominent legal experts and developers have raised red flags. Critics warn that relying on specific block builders to enforce these rules could introduce centralization risks, making protocols effectively freezable and opening the door to backdoor censorship. Striking the right balance between robust network security and absolute decentralization remains one of crypto’s toughest challenges. Do you think automated security circuit breakers are a necessary evolution for DeFi, or a threat to censorship resistance? Drop your perspective in the comments! 📊💡 # Crypto Threads

text: Show HN: Nunya – A "digital privacy screen" that makes text illegible from afar. Hello! I'm Marc. I've built "Nunya", which is a sort of "digital privacy screen". It redraws text to make it readable when looking at your monitor or phone from a normal distance, while making it hard to read by someone who might be looking over your shoulder. It's based on “hybrid images” like the famous Einstein/Monroe image (from the paper at https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1141911.1141919 ) and I thought it'd make a great way to mask text on your phone that you don't want someone nearby reading. I particularly spent time on the transition - I wanted the text to be incredibly legible when close, but incredibly illegible when being far, and tried to optimise for a minimal transition between the two. Demos can be seen at my site for it here: https://usenunya.com I first released this over ten years ago as "PrivacyMessage" (my app names have definitely improved) when Apple first allowed iMessage apps. This was my first app geared towards the general market as I've spent the last 13 years developing iOS apps for a fairly niche market. I'm happy to have brought it back as “Nunya”, and have currently made it available in three forms: - Nunya for Messages (iPhone) I first remade my iMessage app and gave it a bit more polish. It's free for 5 sends, and then $4.99 for a permanent unlock. - Potfolio (iPhone) I then figured Nunya would make for a great flagship feature in a "wealth tracking" finance app I was already working on, so anyone who might glance at your phone when on public transport can't quite see your bank balances. It's currently free (though I might add some new features with IAPs to it later). - Nunya for Chrome A friend then suggested it'd make for a great Chrome extension to be used on all sites. It's free to hide money amounts, and £10 (around $13) to unlock it to work with more (bank details, bitcoin addresses, etc). You can try it here: https://usenunya.com/chrome This is my first real attempt at making apps for a wider market. It's also my very first Chrome extension, and I'm not entirely sure how best to price each of these, nor how to best gate their features. I don't particularly like subscriptions if I can avoid them. I'm curious to hear any thoughts. Particularly: do you think these pricing models are reasonable? I also wonder if Nunya would make for a good feature elsewhere. With more staff working remotely who might be in transit or in cafes, I can imagine businesses could be keen for their staff to use it on more sensitive data. Does that seem plausible? Thanks all.
title: Show HN: Nunya – A "digital privacy screen" that makes text illegible from afar

text: JPMorgan, Visa, Mastercard say third-party vendors targeted in cyberattack. > Nov 19 (Reuters) - JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N), opens new tab, the largest US lender, said on Thursday that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyberattack. > "Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names ‌and email addresses," a JPMorgan spokesperson said, adding that the company would be contacting the affected customers directly. > > Jumpstart your morning with the latest legal news delivered straight to your inbox from The Daily Docket newsletter. Sign up here. > "There is no connection to service disruption of some customers experienced earlier this week," the spokesperson added. > > Earlier this week, the bank experienced problems processing transactions due to a software bug which also affected other banks and caused some disruptions. > > These incidents at JPMorgan followed several other recent problems including a nationwide FAA ground stop that disrupted travel last week and Microsoft's global email outage, while last month crypto exchange Binance experienced a massive hack. > > After the outage, lenders received inquiries from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, according to a ⁠an industry executive, who added that the US banking regulator was trying to assess the impact and wanted to know about communication to customers. > > The Treasury and the OCC were calling banks minutes after the incident was reported to check that the issue was contained and it was not a cyber-related incident, a second person said adding that the OCC routinely checks after any such incidents. > > "Customers don't distinguish between a bank and a vendor when it comes to a cyberattack, so there is a question of reputational risk here," said Carissa Robb at SolomonEdwards, a consulting firm. "There needs to be a little bit more pressure on how often companies are scrutinizing the amount of data that is shared with vendors and the necessity of the data being shared," Robb said. > > A cyber extortion group called "n0n" claimed on November 16 to have obtained cardmember engagement records that included "hundreds of thousands of campaign interactions for tens of thousands of distinct cardmember email addresses," according to a screenshot of the ‌message captured ⁠by cybercrime research platform eCrime.ch. > > The data includes what appears to be 124 bank employee email addresses and more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some with phone numbers and postal codes, according to a Reuters review. Reuters could not independently verify the authenticity of the data. > > JPMorgan declined to comment on the data. > The same hacking group on November 16 posted similar claims regarding Visa and Mastercard and posted data. > > A Visa spokesperson said the company is aware of the claims and that they are "associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. ⁠Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected." > > A Mastercard spokesperson said the company was recently informed of an incident "at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses — non-payments information — from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program. There is no impact ⁠to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards." > > The Visa data posted by the group appears to be primarily focused on Asian-Pacific markets, including Hong Kong, Taiwan, Korea, Japan, Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Australia, Macau and others, according to a Reuters review. Across several spreadsheets, the data includes thousands of purported ⁠customer email addresses, phone numbers, and Visa marketing campaign data. Reuters has not verified the authenticity of the data. > > The Mastercard data posted by n0n includes marketing data related to customers in North America, the Middle East and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses. > > The hacking group has claimed roughly 200 incidents since emerging in September 2026, according to eCrime.ch. > > Reporting by Arasu Kannagi Basil in Bengaluru; Editing by Leroy Leo, Chizu Nomiyama and Nick Zieminski
title: JPMorgan, Visa, Mastercard say third-party vendors targeted in cyberattack

text: As traditional giants rush into digital dollars, USDD’s Yvonne Chia explains why 24/7 access, self-custody, and transparent yield give decentralized stablecoins an edge banks can’t replicate. 20 November – Road Town, Totorla, British Virgin Islands – Decentralized stablecoin protocol USDD is accelerating its multichain utility across TRON, Ethereum, and BNB Chain—combining automated sUSDD yield via its Smart Allocator with GasFree zero-TRX transfers—as traditional financial giants race to build competing stablecoin rails. In a recent industry interview with instant exchange partner ChangeNOW, USDD Head of Communications Yvonne Chia outlined why self-custody, 24/7 settlement, and transparent onchain reserves give decentralized digital dollars a structural advantage over bank-issued alternatives. 1. Permissionless Access vs. Gatekept Accounts For billions of people globally, opening and maintaining a traditional bank account still involves paperwork, minimum balance requirements, geographic restrictions, and approval delays. Even when banks integrate stablecoin rails behind the scenes, those services remain gated behind legacy compliance walls and intermediary control. Crypto-native stablecoins flip that model on its head. As Yvonne Chia highlighted during the interview: “Compare this to a stablecoin like USDD, where all you need is a phone, a working internet connection, you can immediately start a wallet and you have access to your funds right away.” With USDD, users can access and manage their digital dollars directly through their own wallets, without depending on traditional financial intermediaries. This represents a fundamental shift in financial access: users are no longer limited to the services, operating hours, or account structures of a single institution. Instead, they have the freedom to hold, manage, and transfer their assets on their own terms. Self-custody also gives users greater autonomy over their financial decisions. They can choose which wallets to use, where to transfer their assets, and which supported decentralized applications to interact with, without needing to route every transaction through a centralized financial institution. With USDD, users’ digital dollars can move with them across an open blockchain ecosystem, rather than remaining tied to a particular bank or service provider. 2. 24/7 Global Settlement vs. “Banking Hours” Legacy payment networks still operate on decades-old schedules: weekend cutoffs, bank holidays, and multi-day cross-border settlement delays accompanied by hefty wire fees. Blockchain networks never close. Whether it is a Sunday night or a public holiday, USDD moves globally without depending on traditional banking operating hours or settlement windows. “We are able to have transfers 24/7 and we’re not limited to any traditional banking hours. So I think that in some ways, stablecoins are not just becoming banks, but exceeding what traditional banks can offer to users.” To make everyday transfers even smoother than fintech apps, USDD introduced GasFree integration on TRON, allowing users on supported wallets to pay network fees directly in USDD without needing to hold TRX. This removes another practical barrier to stablecoin adoption: having to acquire and maintain a separate gas token just to transfer digital dollars. With GasFree, eligible users can pay approximately 0.5 USDD per transaction, compared with around 1.5 USDT for a standard USDT transfer under the referenced fee conditions. These improvements matter because the usefulness of a stablecoin is not determined by its peg alone. Low-cost transfers, straightforward wallet experiences, and around-the-clock availability are what make digital dollars practical for everyday payments and global value transfers. 3. Passing Yield Back to Users vs. Bank Spreads Perhaps the sharpest contrast between banks and decentralized stablecoins lies in how yield is distributed. In traditional banking, institutions take customer deposits, deploy them into yield-generating markets, and retain a significant portion of the returns. Everyday depositors may receive relatively low interest rates, while higher-yielding products often come with eligibility requirements, minimum deposits, or fixed maturity periods. Stablecoins introduce another way to participate in digital-dollar opportunities. Rather than keeping capital entirely within a traditional deposit account, users can access onchain yield opportunities through decentralized protocols and transparent investment mechanisms. USDD was built to return that value directly to holders. Through USDD Earn, users can deposit USDD to receive sUSDD, earning automated, competitive yield powered by our Smart Allocator system, with no fixed lock-up periods restricting access to their capital. For users, the distinction is important: USDD Earn provides access to a productive stablecoin while maintaining flexibility, rather than requiring users to commit their capital to a conventional fixed-term product. 4. Onchain Verification vs. Institutional Trust Traditional banks ask customers to trust closed-door balance sheets and periodic regulatory filings—until a crisis proves otherwise. USDD takes a different approach through its “Don’t trust, verify” ethos, emphasizing publicly accessible onchain information and independent verification. text: **Libertarian police** I was shooting heroin and reading “The Fountainhead” in the front seat of my privately owned police cruiser when a call came in. I put a quarter in the radio to activate it. It was the chief. “Bad news, detective. We got a situation.” “What? Is the mayor trying to ban trans fats again?” “Worse. Somebody just stole four hundred and forty-seven million dollars’ worth of bitcoins.” The heroin needle practically fell out of my arm. “What kind of monster would do something like that? Bitcoins are the ultimate currency: virtual, anonymous, stateless. They represent true economic freedom, not subject to arbitrary manipulation by any government. Do we have any leads?” “Not yet. But mark my words: we’re going to figure out who did this and we’re going to take them down … provided someone pays us a fair market rate to do so.” “Easy, chief,” I said. “Any rate the market offers is, by definition, fair.” He laughed. “That’s why you’re the best I got, Lisowski. Now you get out there and find those bitcoins.” “Don’t worry,” I said. “I’m on it.” I put a quarter in the siren. Ten minutes later, I was on the scene. It was a normal office building, strangled on all sides by public sidewalks. I hopped over them and went inside. “Home Depot™ Presents the Police!®” I said, flashing my badge and my gun and a small picture of Ron Paul. “Nobody move unless you want to!” They didn’t. “Now, which one of you punks is going to pay me to investigate this crime?” No one spoke up. “Come on,” I said. “Don’t you all understand that the protection of private property is the foundation of all personal liberty?” It didn’t seem like they did. “Seriously, guys. Without a strong economic motivator, I’m just going to stand here and not solve this case. Cash is fine, but I prefer being paid in gold bullion or autographed Penn Jillette posters.” Nothing. These people were stonewalling me. It almost seemed like they didn’t care that a fortune in computer money invented to buy drugs was missing. I figured I could wait them out. I lit several cigarettes indoors. A pregnant lady coughed, and I told her that secondhand smoke is a myth. Just then, a man in glasses made a break for it. “Subway™ Eat Fresh and Freeze, Scumbag!®” I yelled. Too late. He was already out the front door. I went after him. “Stop right there!” I yelled as I ran. He was faster than me because I always try to avoid stepping on public sidewalks. Our country needs a private-sidewalk voucher system, but, thanks to the incestuous interplay between our corrupt federal government and the public-sidewalk lobby, it will never happen. I was losing him. “Listen, I’ll pay you to stop!” I yelled. “What would you consider an appropriate price point for stopping? I’ll offer you a thirteenth of an ounce of gold and a gently worn ‘Bob Barr ‘08’ extra-large long-sleeved men’s T-shirt!” He turned. In his hand was a revolver that the Constitution said he had every right to own. He fired at me and missed. I pulled my own gun, put a quarter in it, and fired back. The bullet lodged in a U.S.P.S. mailbox less than a foot from his head. I shot the mailbox again, on purpose. “All right, all right!” the man yelled, throwing down his weapon. “I give up, cop! I confess: I took the bitcoins.” “Why’d you do it?” I asked, as I slapped a pair of Oikos™ Greek Yogurt Presents Handcuffs® on the guy. “Because I was afraid.” “Afraid?” “Afraid of an economic future free from the pernicious meddling of central bankers,” he said. “I’m a central banker.” I wanted to coldcock the guy. Years ago, a central banker killed my partner. Instead, I shook my head. “Let this be a message to all your central-banker friends out on the street,” I said. “No matter how many bitcoins you steal, you’ll never take away the dream of an open society based on the principles of personal and economic freedom.” He nodded, because he knew I was right. Then he swiped his credit card to pay me. * [Tom O’Donnell](https://www.newyorker.com/humor/daily-shouts/l-p-d-libertarian-police-department)

text: Since all BitcoinCash transactions are broadcast publicly, you can monitor the network and build fun interpretations of the data, visually and with sound. Sites like this have been around for a while, but I'll bet this is the first microtonal one with ghosts. It has a meditative, ambient sort of atmosphere, with clock-like chimes that can occasionally blend together into a single deep, brilliant tone. The geeky microtonal details: Each output of a transaction sounds a chime. The fundamental pitch of the chime is determined by the amount of BCH in that output. On a logarithmic scale, the amounts are mapped to the harmonics of 30 Hz, starting at the second harmonic for dust amounts (546 sats), up to 2100 BCH where it maxes out at the 31st harmonic. (So each harmonic has a range of output sizes that could trigger it. It's not fully continuous with output amount.) A chime's overtones are also selected from harmonics of a 30 Hz fundamental. I simply pick the harmonics that are closest to the frequency ratios of the overtones of an ideal metal bar. That does mean that chimes with fundamentals tuned to lower harmonics of 30 Hz will deviate more from those "ideal" (inharmonic) ratios compared to higher ones (since lower harmonics are further apart in pitch, so you have less resolution), but that was fine with me and I like the end result. I find it very meditative, like you're chilling in the clock dimension. When enough outputs of different sizes are triggered at the same time, you start to hear that warbly, inner-ear harmonic series buzz and the phantom fundamental tone, 30 Hz. Whenever a block (as in "blockchain") arrives, a bright timbre with harmonic overtones is sounded at 30 Hz, unifying the soundscape, if you will. There are lots of visual representations of the transaction data too. Each transaction is represented by a spirit whose size is determined by the transaction's size (in bytes, not amount sent). Their lantern color is determined by fee-rate (satoshis/byte), and each output is represented by a suitcase. Features like fungible tokens, NFTs, and OP_RETURN usage are indicated with various accessories. This was a fun opportunity to combine two things I'm extremely geeky about. I put it together for a Hackathon, but I'm sure I'll keep improving it. Thanks for reading!

text: > I've stopped trusting any of these influencer-benchmaxxers The influencer competition for attention in the LLM space is wild. LLMs have emerged as the topic of 2026, so all of the influencers who were previously scattered around topics like web dev, backend dev, product management, cryptocurrency, and every other niche have all pivoted into the same LLM influencer space. It’s like one big cage match where they’re all becoming increasingly cutthroat to fight for the dwindling scraps of attention in a crowded space. For the first half of this year it was interesting to see most of them move in unison on the hot topic of the moment, competing to have the best guides, hottest takes, and best courses (which are always shockingly expensive and no better than free content, but they encourage everyone to get their employers to pay). It was fascinating to watch them jump from topic to topic together, like when OpenClaw took off and they all had guides on personal agents or even created their own competing OpenClaw project. Or when MCP was the topic and everyone had the Ultimate Guide to MCP. Then some time this year everyone realized the space was too crowded and switch to contrarian hot takes: Every new model release had influencers making videos about how it was terrible, awful, and shouldn’t have been released. All of the old buzzwords got new videos like MCP IS DEAD with influencers going in the opposite direction of what they said 6 months ago. And now, the interpersonal drama is taking over. People like Theo are posting attacks and threats on others or bragging about blocking or getting blocked, which is the absolute last thing I want to read from supposed experts on a topic. Most sane people opt out of the influencer content after they realize how much it’s clickbait over quality, but all of these people also have rabid fan bases of people who can’t get enough drama and contrarian hot takes. It can be hard to filter out the contrarian hot takes when they get dressed up as new benchmarks or supposed revelations (declaring a model has been nerfed is evergreen) and cross posted to other sites.

text: $ETH.X Most self-proclaimed traders build their entire strategy around lagging indicators, mistakenly treating historical price data as a crystal ball for future market movements. Tools like moving averages, MACD, and RSI are mathematically designed to confirm trends that have already begun, not predict where price is heading next. By the time a golden cross appears or an oscillator signals overbought conditions, institutional algorithms and smart money have already captured the bulk of the move and are preparing to exit. Relying exclusively on these rearview-mirror metrics forces retail traders into a perpetual cycle of chasing momentum; buying near the top of a rally and selling at the bot

text: JPMorgan Puts Bitcoin Production Cost at $86,000 a Coin JPMorgan has lifted its estimate of what it costs to produce a single bitcoin to roughly $86,000, while the coin itself trades tens of thousands of dollars below that level. The figure comes from a bank report dated November 18, led by analyst Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou. It has climbed steadily through the year: $77,000 to $78,000 in June, about $85,000 by September. The market moved the other way. Bitcoin sat near $65,000 when the report was published and slipped below $60,000 two days later, widening the shortfall on every coin mined to more than $26,000. JPMorgan is careful with the number. It calls production cost a "soft floor" rather than a hard support level, because miners do not simply stop the moment a coin is worth less than its average cost of extraction. What the bank expects instead is adjustment: higher-cost miners selling part of their reserves to fund operations; some operators redirecting power and hardware toward AI infrastructure; weaker miners shutting down, which lowers hashrate and eventually pulls difficulty, and average cost, down. That last mechanism carries the argument. A sustained decline in hashrate would be evidence of capitulation, and JPMorgan's framework treats it as the path to cost relief even without a price recovery. The report also links the recent weakness to retail outflows from bitcoin and ether exchange-traded funds, together with shifting expectations around interest rate cuts. There is a feedback risk in the short term. Miners that sell reserves to stay afloat add supply to a market that is already short of demand. For anyone following the network, three signals matter from here: hashrate, difficulty adjustments, and ETF flows. 📷 Marko Ahtisaari · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons 🔗 Source: Crypto Briefing # Bitcoin # Crypto # Lightning

text: The # blockchain # tech itself is immaterial. The details don't matter. One could implement a "digital currency" and keep track of its transactions in some other way, but no matter the implementation it's still wholly dependent upon the illusion of virtuality, the false notion that the world of computing is somehow independent of the compulsory nature of corporations backed by governments. But let's assume for the sake of argument that it was somehow possible to implement such a system in an independent way. The easiest way would be to dispose of computers altogether and thus dispense of the extreme complexity of manufacturing them and maintaining them and interconnecting them, and implement an independent currency through physical means. Such a system could work: one could invent a totally independent currency that held good only within the limited scope of those people willing to honor the new currency's value. But this is NOT how # cryptocurrency is intended to work; it's certainly not how crypto is marketed. The dipshit Alyx ran into was spouting (on their blog) the typical crypto sales pitch--selling their blockchain trash by hyping it up as a good investment that was likely to increase in value, contrasting against evil Uncle Sam fiat petrodollars. But what is an # investment in the first place? It's something that's intended to be cashed out--in terms of hard currency, i.e. evil Uncle Sam fiat petrodollars. Without that possibility of converting crypto to real money, the techbro interest in the stuff would be practically nil.

It should be obvious enough that there's nothing genuinely novel or innovative about blockchain garbage (leaving aside the novelty of having the garbage be defined in software) from reading news articles about crypto: the shit is continued to be reckoned as valuable and a worthwhile financial instrument ONLY because rich and powerful people are dabbling in the stuff. Elite gamblers in dodgy investments are far better placed to profit upon them, and better able to absorb losses when an investment scam collapses. These elite crypto players furnish the only really credible offramp out of the crypto sphere: the superior ability of these rich crypto gamblers to cash out when they want is what sustains the whole bubble. If they all took their money and fled, cryptocurrency will simply bottom out as an "investment."

But the third-of-its-kind event, hosted at Trump’s Northern Virginia golf club, isn’t exactly a hot ticket. Nor is it popular among some in the president’s inner circle. Much like his political stock, the value of the president’s digital token has deteriorated. Trump’s first meme coin dinner, in April 2025, saw investors spending some $148 million in a contest to dine with the president, according to the cryptocurrency intelligence firm Inca Digital. Sunday’s dinner, which invites the top 185 investors in $TRUMP coin, showed closing numbers of only $8.6 million, according to a Reuters report.

text: Malicious Ad Campaign Used iPhone Exploits to Hunt Wallet Seed Phrases A malvertising operation spent roughly six months turning ordinary online ads into a delivery system for iOS exploits, and crypto wallets were the prize. Confiant researchers, who call the campaign MoldyRoost, published their findings on Nov 20. The operation ran from May 12 to Nov 17, 2026 and was tied to more than 480 ad domains split across six clusters of activity. One cluster did most of the work: 403 domains, aimed mainly at Hong Kong, Japan and Singapore. The wider reach covered iPhones in 47 countries. What makes it uncomfortable is how little the victim had to do: A single tap on a programmatic ad opened a landing page built by the operators. That page delivered its code as it loaded — no download, no prompt, no second tap. Once inside, the implant searched Notes, messages, saved images and keychain data for wallet recovery phrases. The toolkit was aimed at iOS 13 through 17.2.1: 23 exploits arranged into five chains. Six further vulnerabilities targeted iOS 18.4 to 18.7, and three of them were zero-days at the time they were used. Confiant groups the exploit families under names such as Coruna and DarkSword; together the set covers 29 vulnerabilities across the older iOS releases. The implant looked for seed phrases belonging to MetaMask, Phantom and Trust Wallet — not because those apps were broken, but because of what people keep around them. A QR code sitting in a screenshot was as useful to the attackers as a note file. That is the detail worth sitting with. The weakness lived in Apple's operating system, not in the wallets. The practical response is unglamorous. Fully updated iPhones appear to be outside this campaign's reach, which puts patching ahead of any app-level fix. Seed phrases do not belong in Notes, in chat threads or in a camera roll. MoldyRoost is less a crypto story than a reminder of where the attack surface actually sits: the page you landed on for two seconds, and the file you saved two years ago. 📷 Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons 🔗 Source: Crypto Briefing # Crypto # Blockchain # Bitcoin

text: Ethereum Treasury Firm BTCS Sells Over Half of Its ETH Holdings for $43.8M to Repay Aave Debt Ethereum treasury firm BTCS sold approximately 27,300 ETH, representing more than half of its holdings, for $43.8 million on November 20 at an average price of $1,604, according to an SEC filing. The proceeds were used to repay Aave loans, reducing its outstanding debt by 81% to $10.5 million and lowering its loan-to-value ratio to 32%. As of November 22, BTCS still held approximately 24,245 ETH, with combined cash and digital assets valued at $61 million. Amid market volatility, its DeFi unit Imperium temporarily withdrew from liquidity pools and plans to redeploy capital when conditions improve. —

text: I think you missed the point of the comment. Yes, it's set up to be a market. But unlike say the stock market, where people try to do price discovery through analysis, prediction markets have been shown to have a vast majority of losers, and very few winners. It's more like a casino than a market, in its result. Though the house is this case is distributed. And really, the point from the parent comment that it's a way to monetize non-financial insider information is way more true than it's not. Prediction markets have turned out to not surface "predictions" so much as incentivizing people who factually know, to gain. The stock market lets me monetize a good guess, or my predictive research. "Prediction" markets are not about predictions. Unlike regular markets. Insider information on financials is way more controlled, too. If I had access to the next earning report and I trade on it, that's not really a "prediction", is it? Prediction markets are more like how bitcoin proves that nobody has a full quantum computer yet. It would just be too tempting to use it to steal bitcoins, as a converging instrumental goal.

text: Mining is one. This tweet is misleading, cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin are designed to work this way - the difficult of mining a coin automatically adjusts to be slightly less costly than buying a coin, giving miners a slim profit margin. Whenever the price drops some of those miners will no longer be profitable and they'll stop mining until the difficulty adjusts again or the price goes back up. Other network validation activities that can earn a return are staking, running masternodes for specialized networks (providing services or participating in governance), or operating mining pools. You can rent out storage capacity on decentralized storage networks or rent out spare CPU/GPU resources for distributed computing, provide services like blockchain data availability, or run other infrastructure such as indexes or RPC endpoints. Some protocols provide compensation for governance participation. You can lend it to borrowers to collect interest, provide liquidity for DeFi to get a share of trading fees, or provide liquidity to stabletokens to get return from trading fees or protocol incentives. A lot of this is very complicated, though, so people tend not to pay as much attention to it. "Buy low sell high" is easy to understand.

text: OK, well I appreciate that. Pretty much the main point is that it's *not* controlled by anyone. It can't be. There is no company, no leader, no nothing. So one of the major differences is that when the US, or Canadian, or Turkemenistanian or whatever government needs more dollars, it can print them. So if there's 4.1 trillion in circulation and they need money for whatever purpose (usually monetary control) they can just inject say 500 billion and now the economy has 4.6 trillion in it and everyone's dollar is worth less (this is inflation). Crude explanation but covers what's important. Bitcoin is capped at 21 million by design. For more technical explanation you can read into it more, but that's the reality. People will claim anyone can just change it but again, they don't know what they're talking about. What the technical argument against that doesn't cover, game theory does). So 21 million bitcoin, millions already lost (user issue not bitcoin issue), there will never be any more. And fiat currencies keep inflating by design and we're headed for huge climate change related inflation among other current sources of inflationary pressure. If the Dow is at 200,000 is that still good if a carton of eggs is $40? If you think wages will keep up, more power to you. I prefer to at least keep a little currency that no central power can control. Gold is nice too for many of the same reasons, and Bitcoin is not a replacement. But very different use cases. And ultimately, gold supply is not really capped. For the right price there's more to be found. Bitcoin? Well 18 years no one has been able to find a single extra satoshi over what should be out there. Despite ample reasons to try (if possible).

text: I mean, the article you posted doesn't address everything in my previous post. I'm still waiting for more info before conceding anything about how useful LLMs are in mathematical proofs specifically. As for the wider question about whether LLMs are "powerful" (whatever that's supposed to mean exactly)... I'm sure you must remember some of the ridiculous claims that were made about how Blockchain was going to change the world. Not only was it going to revolutionize how you payed for your groceries, but your house title would be on the blockchain, you'd use NFTs to get into venues, you could own NFTs for pieces of the Mona Lisa, Zuck's "The Metaverse(tm)" where you'd work your day job in the future, you'd vote in governmental elections using a blockchain and your wallet private key, you'd have your recovery passphrase stamped in solid metal buried in your back yard, and your biometrics data had to be on the blockchain for some dumbass reason. And all these revolutions were perpetually just a little ways off in the future. "Web3" they called it. At this point, most people look back on anything blockchain-related with embarrassment. The last time blockchain made the news was the last time someone in the Trump family ran another blockchain-related scam. Nobody has buttonholed me to tell me I should be mining Ethereum or whatever in quite a while. And nobody has asked in my employer's IT department all-hands meeting when the company is going to offer customers the option to pay with Bitcoin in a long time. The price of Bitcoin is still relatively high surprisingly and Tether hasn't collapsed to zero or anything yet, but the pool of people who still put any stock whatsoever in anything blockchain related is increasingly confined to weird little echo chambers that nobody else takes seriously. And it's clear at this point that blockchain is never going to be anything but a cringe gambling platform. (Let me pause at this point to say if you're still emotionally invested in anything blockchain-related, we might as well end this conversation here because it's clear there's no hope for ever reaching any consensus.) And guess who brought you the AI bubble. Sam Altman was the one behind [Worldcoin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_(blockchain)), that biometrics-on-the-blockchain thing I mentioned in the previous paragraph. CoreWeave was a cryptocurrency-mining company. Elon Musk. Donald Trump. When the snakeoil salesman gets outed as a fraud and then comes back a decade later with an ostrich oil concoction (that *definitely* isn't just overpriced mineral oil) that'll cure your sleep apnea 100% for sure this time I swear, the proper response is a whole lot of skepticism. And they're making the same kind of outlandish claims about AI as they did about blockchain. 10x/100x. Photoshop clones. Train an AI to act like you so your family can keep talking to you after you die. You can let the agent make restaurant reservations for you, no supervision needed; the restaurant won't even be able to tell it's an agent. Videos of 6-monitor computers running futuristic-looking "dashboards" overviewing the extremely profitable enterprise that "Jarvis" supposedly created/maintains autonomously for the video's creator. Remember that thing where they were going to recreate Minecraft and Doom except every frame was just Stable Diffusion output and there was no persistent game world or engine behind it beyond the user's key presses being fed to the image generator somehow? What did they call that, "vibegaming" or something? Not to mention TESCREAL or trying to convince religious leaders that Claude is conscious or AI doomerism claims like "X% chance it'll extinct humanity". Meanwhile, as I mentioned in my previous post, aside from *maybe* the mathematical proofs, there's currently no reason to think anyone's ever gotten any benefit out of an LLM beyond anecdotes. And enough of those are clearly delusional that it's worth scrutinizing the maybe-less-unhinged-sounding ones. That's largely why these claims about mathematical proofs seem so suspicious to me. Software development teams using LLMs are *less* productive and have more outages. Everything in entertainment with even a faint whiff of slop elicits only hatred from normies. OpenAI, Anthropic, even Google are losing *ridiculous* amounts of money on LLMs with no sign of profitability in sight. They're having to subsidize their own users to get anyone to use products like ChatGPT and Claude. Local LLMs aren't much cheaper if at all. Even if LLMs *were* useful, they'd be prohibitively expensive if they weren't subsidized. And yet, after a million different claims about LLMs being useful turned out to be hogwash, I'm supposed to believe this one? Of course, I will when there's sufficient evidence, but I've seen similar claims turn out to be laughably and obviously false to take this one with a salt lick. So, I hope that all makes it clear why I'm skeptical of the mathematical proof claims. And any other claims that LLMs are "useful". But back to your core question. "What would it take for your to believe that LLMs are actually incredibly powerful?" Again, it really depends what you mean by "powerful". I mean, if they could do things reliably without a human there to correct them (without ending up in the national news, that is) or if it could be demonstrated that it could make people actually more productive without making them stupid or the product inferior or if it could enable people to do worthwhile things that nobody could do before *and* if it could do at least one of those things at a cost that wasn't prohibitive (without being subsidized), then I'd admit it was at least to some extent "useful". The whole "making people stupid" thing in particular makes me extremely reticent to *ever* voluntarily touch an LLMs with a 10ft pole even if I believed them to be useful. Not saying I'd keep refusing to do so if my boss made my paycheck contingent on using them. I'm lucky not to be in that position. But I've built a career on my smarts. And nothing I've seen about LLMs leads me to think I won't need those smarts in the future. Quite the opposite. Fixing the slop (as Cory Doctorow calls it, "the digital asbestos we're shoveling into our walls") after bosses figure out it needs fixed is going to require a lot of problem-solving skill. And the ones who haven't succumbed to LLM-induced learned helplessness are going to be more effective at that than the ones who have. Plus, the kind of fun I like to have outside of work is the kind of fun that requires flexing my brain a lot. If I surrendered my brain to the LLMs, I'd lose basically *the* part of myself that I most value. And not just because it's the part I can wield to get a paycheck by delivering value to shareholders. Because it's a big part of what makes me me. It's core to my identity, and necessary to the things that give me joy. Aside from all that, I find LLMs unethical and would avoid using them on that basis. They give people I've never met asthma, contribute to global warming, consume shit-tons of water, and destroy ecosystems for huge data centers.

text: I was shooting heroin and reading “The Fountainhead” in the front seat of my privately owned police cruiser when a call came in. I put a quarter in the radio to activate it. It was the chief. “Bad news, detective. We got a situation.” “What? Is the mayor trying to ban trans fats again?” “Worse. Somebody just stole four hundred and forty-seven million dollars’ worth of bitcoins.” The heroin needle practically fell out of my arm. “What kind of monster would do something like that? Bitcoins are the ultimate currency: virtual, anonymous, stateless. They represent true economic freedom, not subject to arbitrary manipulation by any government. Do we have any leads?” “Not yet. But mark my words: we’re going to figure out who did this and we’re going to take them down … provided someone pays us a fair market rate to do so.” “Easy, chief,” I said. “Any rate the market offers is, by definition, fair.” He laughed. “That’s why you’re the best I got, Lisowski. Now you get out there and find those bitcoins.” “Don’t worry,” I said. “I’m on it.” I put a quarter in the siren. Ten minutes later, I was on the scene. It was a normal office building, strangled on all sides by public sidewalks. I hopped over them and went inside. “Home Depot™ Presents the Police!®” I said, flashing my badge and my gun and a small picture of Ron Paul. “Nobody move unless you want to!” They didn’t. “Now, which one of you punks is going to pay me to investigate this crime?” No one spoke up. “Come on,” I said. “Don’t you all understand that the protection of private property is the foundation of all personal liberty?” It didn’t seem like they did. “Seriously, guys. Without a strong economic motivator, I’m just going to stand here and not solve this case. Cash is fine, but I prefer being paid in gold bullion or autographed Penn Jillette posters.” Nothing. These people were stonewalling me. It almost seemed like they didn’t care that a fortune in computer money invented to buy drugs was missing. I figured I could wait them out. I lit several cigarettes indoors. A pregnant lady coughed, and I told her that secondhand smoke is a myth. Just then, a man in glasses made a break for it. “Subway™ Eat Fresh and Freeze, Scumbag!®” I yelled. Too late. He was already out the front door. I went after him. “Stop right there!” I yelled as I ran. He was faster than me because I always try to avoid stepping on public sidewalks. Our country needs a private-sidewalk voucher system, but, thanks to the incestuous interplay between our corrupt federal government and the public-sidewalk lobby, it will never happen. I was losing him. “Listen, I’ll pay you to stop!” I yelled. “What would you consider an appropriate price point for stopping? I’ll offer you a thirteenth of an ounce of gold and a gently worn ‘Bob Barr ‘08’ extra-large long-sleeved men’s T-shirt!” He turned. In his hand was a revolver that the Constitution said he had every right to own. He fired at me and missed. I pulled my own gun, put a quarter in it, and fired back. The bullet lodged in a U.S.P.S. mailbox less than a foot from his head. I shot the mailbox again, on purpose. “All right, all right!” the man yelled, throwing down his weapon. “I give up, cop! I confess: I took the bitcoins.” “Why’d you do it?” I asked, as I slapped a pair of Oikos™ Greek Yogurt Presents Handcuffs® on the guy. “Because I was afraid.” “Afraid?” “Afraid of an economic future free from the pernicious meddling of central bankers,” he said. “I’m a central banker.” I wanted to coldcock the guy. Years ago, a central banker killed my partner. Instead, I shook my head. “Let this be a message to all your central-banker friends out on the street,” I said. “No matter how many bitcoins you steal, you’ll never take away the dream of an open society based on the principles of personal and economic freedom.” He nodded, because he knew I was right. Then he swiped his credit card to pay me.

Basically, before 401ks and other retail investment vehicles appeared, the stock market's primary function was to collect money from large scale investors (banks, insurances and the likes) and put it to productive usage. Boring stuff. But once people's retirements were tied to the stock markets, the stock markets were societally and thus politically forced/incentivized to always go up, and that meant that there suddenly was a large, continuous influx of capital to nowadays the tune of dozens of billions of dollars a month. That in turn meant a huge incentive to siphon tiny margins off of all the trades (which led to HFT being a thing) and a constant incentive for C-level leadership to engage in all kinds of shady deals to appear better to the markets - complex webs of shell companies to avoid taxes, financial fraud, sale-lease-back vulturism destroying entire companies... And it turned out, there was so much money flowing into the US retirement savings system that it couldn't be soaked up by the American economy alone, which led to American companies and investment vehicles buying up assets across the world, treating them just the same - and the work we do outside the US is slaving away for some American boomers' retirement. The result of that was eventually the 2007ff financial crisis, where dumbass investments by a single bank was enough to trigger the entire world economy to crash, then we had dumbass money hype up cryptocurrencies, and now we have dumbass money blowing up the AI bubble - which probably will explode much, much harder than 2007ff. text: > You might want to read a bit about Bitcoin scarcity, how it stays scarce and how its scarcity compares to other things. Just being scarce isn't enough though. It has to have fairly universal desire to be owned, meaning people must attribute value to it. There were a limited run of trading cards produced for the 1980s TV show ALF making them pretty scarce, but I think you'll be hard pressed to find someone willing to take ALF cards over gold as a unit of trade. Gold, for better or worse, has a long historical acceptance as a transportable unit of wealth across nations, cultures, and governments. No one needs to be convinced that gold has value, or that it will still have value 50 years from now. So the real question for Bitcoin is: Are the majority of people that hold it truly valuing it as a substitute for a unit of transportable wealth or are they engaged in gambling hoping for *greater fool theory*? I'm sure the answer is "its a mix of both", but it certainly looks like its far fewer true believers and far more get-rich-quick chasers.

text: There's no "design" here. Individual participants make their own investment decisions on building out the servers to mine Bitcoin at scale, and then over the useful life of that hardware it mines Bitcoin when profitable and then the hardware is retired or sold for another purpose once it's no longer profitable. They plan things out with an assumption about energy costs, Bitcoin prices, etc., and sometimes those long term projections turn out to be wrong to where they have to retire the hardware earlier than initially planned, or having a lower utilization rate over the course of its useful life, and they lose money on that. The macro equilibriums make the system as a whole survive, but individual players can and do get wiped out from shifts in prices that break their assumptions. And sometimes it swings the other way, too, where they make windfall profits they weren't expecting.

I decided it was the same risk with Vaultwarden but with more stress on me having to actually maintain it. I'm not sure there really is a good hosted solution that removes that risk. I disabled auto-updating on my extension so at least hopefully I'm running a non-pwned version but at some point you have to update and there is no "lag-time" setting for extensions. I did use KeePassXC years ago but the sync there was always a pain, and you're just back at the "trust random app-store/fdroid developer is a good actor/not compromised" problem and it's probably easier to target one random guy (which might just be, here's a stack of bitcoin, leave your front gate unlocked on the 17th) than a big company who's whole job is password management. Whole thing sucks tbh.
